summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is criminal in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code covers any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural, and the sources disagree on the penalty it carries. Outright International records six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, about US$240 to US$720. The archived text of the 2020 code specifies two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. Human Dignity Trust gives a maximum of three years. A December 2024 press report cites Article 318 as carrying up to five years. The 1982 Penal Code that preceded the current one provided up to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.

Enforcement is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online, described as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 code. In June 2024 two women were detained after asking an imam to marry them; the marriage allegation was not proven in court, but the women said they had previously had sexual relations together. On 12 December 2024 a court convicted them of homosexuality and sentenced them to five and six months respectively. Because the sentences were shorter than the detention already served, they were released. Human Dignity Trust described the conviction as a human rights violation, and it was the first conviction of its kind in the country.

The enforcement picture is not uniform. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report records no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during that year and states that authorities did not actively enforce the law. Police were reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ people, and no such violence was reported in 2023. The same report lists widespread impunity among the country's major human rights problems.

No legal gender-marker change is available to transgender people, and no law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code contains no protections for LGBTQ people.

There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local law has no partner recognition or spousal protections.

Social exposure carries risk. LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the wider population. Discrimination extends to education and employment, and some are ostracised from their homes, neighbourhoods and villages.
tangentialFactors:
Both documented prosecutions arose from exposure rather than surveillance. The 2022 case followed a leaked sexual video, and the 2024 case followed the couple's approach to an imam to marry them.

A 2023 Gallup survey found that 26 percent of respondents said the area where they lived would be a good place for LGBTQ+ people, a 10-point increase on the previous year.

The State Department's 2010 report on Comoros carried limited LGBT content. It documented poor prison conditions, restrictions on movement, press and religion, and discrimination against women, none of which is specific to transgender people.
localsOnly:
The Family Code establishes marriage as the union of a man and a woman, and same-sex couples have no recognised legal rights.

The 2012 Labor Code provides no protections for LGBTQ people, and no non-discrimination law covers gender identity.

Article 5 of Law 86-006/AF of 1986 prohibits organisations founded on an unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose contrary to the law or public morals. No LGBTIQ organisations are known to operate in the country.

The government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct.

Most LGBTQ people do not disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity as of 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty for Article 300 is reported inconsistently. The archived text of the 2020 code specifies two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs; Outright International records six months to two years and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs; Human Dignity Trust gives up to three years; a December 2024 press report cites Article 318 as carrying up to five years. Which provision and range applies in practice is unresolved.

No source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, and no trans-specific violence data for Comoros was identified.

The finding that authorities did not enforce the law in 2023 rests on a single year of official reporting and does not describe enforcement in other years.
